subject: botany
question_text: What is bagging technique? How is it useful in plant breeding programmes?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section (book p.18, SAQ 2). Botany holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. page_header: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants · 4 marks

steps.label: Definition

lines.text: Bagging = covering the emasculated flower of
the female parent with a butter paper bag

lines: It is done during artificial hybridisation,
so no stray pollen lands on the stigma.
steps.why: The definition carries three parts the examiner checks: WHAT (covering with a butter paper bag), WHOM (the emasculated flower of the female parent), and WHEN (during artificial hybridisation).
common_mistakes: Writing 'polythene bag' or just 'a cover' — the stated material is butter paper.
Leaving out 'emasculated' and 'female parent' — bagging follows emasculation on that plant.
steps.memory_tip: Emasculate first, then bag: remove the anthers, then seal the flower.
steps.margin_note: Both boxed lines together are the 2-mark definition — write the material, the flower and the timing.

steps.label: Unisexual flowers
lines: If the female parent bears unisexual flowers,
the female flower buds are bagged without
emasculation — they have no anthers to remove.
steps.why: This special case shows you understand WHY emasculation exists at all: a female flower carries no stamens, so only the bag is needed.
common_mistakes: Emasculating a female flower in the answer — there is nothing to remove.
Bagging after the flower opens. It is the BUD that is bagged.
steps.memory_tip: No anthers → nothing to cut → bag the bud directly.
steps.margin_note: One sentence on the unisexual case — the book states it as its own point.

steps.label: Usefulness
lines: The bag keeps unwanted pollen off the stigma.
When the stigma matures, only the chosen
pollen is dusted on it and the flower is

steps.why: The use is contamination control: the breeder decides the male parent, so every seed formed is the intended cross, which is the whole point of a breeding programme.
common_mistakes: Saying the bag 'protects the flower from insects' as the purpose — the purpose is pollen control.
Forgetting that the flower is rebagged after dusting the chosen pollen.
steps.memory_tip: Bag → dust chosen pollen → rebag. The stigma only ever meets the pollen the breeder picked.
steps.margin_note: Link the bag to the desired-character cross — that link is the mark.

insider_note: Say 'butter paper bag', not just 'bag' — examiners look for the specific material as evidence the technique was actually studied.
